title: Robots and Roots
summary: A web server politely lists the folder it wants hidden. One readable backup later, you are signing in; one careless sudo rule later, you are root.
story: Larkspur Studios (made up) runs one web server, web01, on the network 10.10.2.0/24. You start on scout, your Linux box on the same network. Find the server, see what it is trying to hide, and work your way up to root.
goal: Capture the user flag in the deploy account's home folder and the root flag in /root.
skills: port scanning, robots.txt, reading web folders, ssh, sudo -l

hints.text: What to think about first: find the server, then find out what it is quietly trying to keep out of sight. Websites sometimes ask search engines not to look in certain places - and that list is public, so it points straight at the interesting folders.

Find the machine: 'nmap -sn 10.10.2.0/24' lists who answers on the network (no port checks yet). Then 'nmap -sV 10.10.2.30' shows which services it runs: port 80 is a web server. curl is a command-line web browser that prints the page's text: 'curl -s http://10.10.2.30/' (-s just hides the progress bar).

Most websites have a file called robots.txt at the top. It tells search engines which folders to skip ('Disallow: /something/'). It isn't a lock - anyone can read it, and anyone can visit the folders it names. Read it: curl -s http://10.10.2.30/robots.txt

Visit the folder that robots.txt names (curl -s http://10.10.2.30/FOLDER/). Inside is a deploy note with the password of the 'deploy' account. Sign in with ssh: 'ssh deploy@10.10.2.30', yes to the new-host question, then the password. 'cat flag.txt' shows the user flag.

Now 'sudo -l' shows what deploy may run as root: awk. awk is a small text-processing language that reads any file it is given, and under sudo it reads it as root. So: sudo awk '{ print }' /root/flag.txt prints root's flag ('{ print }' means print every line). A tool that reads files or runs programs should never be on a sudo list.
